title: Nearby Friends
problem: Design a system like Facebook Nearby Friends / Snap Map that shows you which of your friends are nearby in near-real-time.
summary: A location-sharing system where each client publishes its GPS coordinates every ~30 seconds over a long-lived WebSocket and receives updates for friends that have opted in. The dominant design choice is an asymmetric fan-out: writes are O(1) into Redis GEO, reads are a pub/sub fan-out driven by the friend graph, with Kafka as the durable backbone between location publishers and per-subscriber WebSocket senders. The main tradeoff is freshness vs cost — publishing every 30s is 6x cheaper than every 5s but shifts the UI toward 'approximate nearby' rather than 'live'. Sized for ~200M DAU and ~100M concurrent WebSocket connections.

functional: Accept location pings from online users over a persistent WebSocket connection.
Broadcast each ping to the user's friends who are (a) online, (b) within a configurable radius, (c) not hidden from this user.
Let a user toggle invisible mode instantly; in-flight pings must not leak after toggle.
Let friends subscribe to a user's live location for a bounded session (e.g. 1 hour).
Expose a REST 'last known location' endpoint for offline friends with opt-in.
nonFunctional: End-to-end ping-to-friend latency under 2 s at p99.
Support 100M monthly active users, 10M concurrent WebSockets per region.
Location history retention is zero by default; only the latest ping is stored.
Privacy toggles must propagate within 500 ms across all connected fanout nodes.
Graceful degradation: if the fanout cluster is down, pings are dropped, not queued.
Backpressure protects the server when a user has 5000 friends watching.

assumptions: Average friend list size = 200; nearby-friends opt-in = 10% of graph → ~20 subscribers per publisher
Location publish cadence = every 30s per active client
Location precision = ~10m (6 decimal places of lng/lat)
estimates: WebSocket servers: 100M / 50K per node ≈ 2000 WS nodes
Redis GEO memory: 100M keys * ~100B ≈ 10 GB (sharded across 20 shards at 500MB each)
Kafka throughput: 3.3M * 200B ≈ 660 MB/s sustained, 2 GB/s peak

architecture.mermaid: graph LR client[Client] --> lb[Connection LB] lb --> ws[WebSocket Server] ws --> pub[Location Publisher] pub --> geo[(Redis GEO)] pub --> kafka[Location Stream] kafka --> sub[Subscription Manager] sub --> friends[Friends Service] sub --> ws ws --> notif[Notification Service]

client.name: Client (iOS / Android)
client.summary: Mobile app holding a persistent WebSocket, publishing its location every 30s and rendering friends' positions on a map.

sections.heading: Responsibilities
sections.body:
- Acquire GPS fix (CLLocationManager / FusedLocationProvider)
- Open WSS to the WebSocket server and send {type:LOC, lat, lng, ts} every 30s
- Receive FRIEND_LOC frames and update map pins
- Throttle in background (iOS significant-location-change, Android passive provider) to protect battery

sections.heading: Why 30 seconds
sections.body: Facebook's published cadence. At walking speed (1.4 m/s) a user moves ~42m in 30s — smaller than the 'nearby' radius by 2 orders of magnitude, so freshness is sufficient. Going to 5s would cost 6x the bandwidth and battery for no perceivable UX win.

sections.heading: Privacy
sections.body: Opt-in per friendship edge. Client attaches a session token; server re-checks on every publish that sharing is still enabled. Kill switch flushes both sides within one heartbeat.

bottlenecks.title: Battery drain from 30s GPS + WebSocket keepalive
bottlenecks.trigger: Continuous foreground usage: GPS fix every 30s plus WSS heartbeat means the radio and location subsystem never fully sleep. On iOS/Android a high-accuracy fix every 30s burns ~5-10% battery/hour.
bottlenecks.symptom: Users uninstall after noticing the app is the top battery consumer in Settings > Battery; App Store reviews cite 'kills my phone'.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use significant-location-change / FusedLocationProvider PRIORITY_BALANCED_POWER_ACCURACY when stationary; switch to 20m displacement filter instead of 30s timer; drop to passive provider in background; coalesce WS keepalive to OS-level push (APNs silent push / FCM high-priority) when backgrounded >5 min.
bottlenecks.detection: Client telemetry: battery_delta_per_hour histogram bucketed by app_state (fg/bg); alert if p50 foreground drain >8%/hr. Also iOS MetricKit energyImpact and Android JobScheduler throttling events.

bottlenecks.title: GPS accuracy and cold-fix latency on publish
bottlenecks.trigger: Indoors or in urban canyons, GPS accuracy degrades to 50-200m and cold fix can take 10-30s — longer than the 30s publish interval. Client publishes either stale or low-quality coordinates, violating the 10m precision assumption.
bottlenecks.symptom: Friends see pins jumping across blocks, snapping to highways, or stuck minutes behind reality; 'nearby' alerts fire for users actually a mile away.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Fuse Wi-Fi/BLE/cell-tower positioning (CoreLocation already does; on Android use FusedLocationProvider); attach accuracy_m to every LOC frame and have server suppress fan-out when accuracy_m > 100; use Kalman filter client-side to smooth jitter; skip publish if delta < accuracy radius.
bottlenecks.detection: Client metric: location_accuracy_m p50/p95 per session; server-side counter of frames dropped due to accuracy > threshold. Alert if p95 accuracy >75m for >5% of sessions.

bottlenecks.title: Reconnect storm on network flap or app resume
bottlenecks.trigger: A WS server dying drops ~50K connections; users on spotty mobile networks flap constantly. Without jitter, clients reconnect in lockstep and hammer the LB/WS tier; at 100M concurrent, even 1% flap/min = 16K reconnects/sec.
bottlenecks.symptom: Spike in 503s at the LB, WS nodes pegged on TLS handshakes, users see 'Connecting...' spinner for 10-30s, friend pins go grey en masse.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Exponential backoff with full jitter (1s → 30s cap, random in [0, backoff]); honor server-sent reconnect-after hint on graceful drain; resume with last-seq cookie so server can skip redelivering LOC frames already seen; cap reconnect attempts and fall back to APNs/FCM silent wake.
bottlenecks.detection: Client metric: reconnect_count per session, time_to_first_frame after reconnect. Server metric: WS handshake QPS per node; alert if handshake_rate > 5x steady-state or if reconnect-after-close < 2s for >10% of clients.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the mobile client is in this design For Nearby Friends, the *whole point* is showing where your friends physically are — and the only thing that knows that is the GPS chip in their phone. The client isn't just a UI; it's the **source of truth for every location** in the system. It has to acquire a GPS fix, decide when a fix is fresh enough to be worth sending, hold a persistent WebSocket so the server can push friends' updates back without polling, and render those updates on a map. The 30-second publish cadence is a client-side decision too — the phone's battery and radio are the scarcest resources in the whole architecture, so the client gets to throttle. ## What happens without a smart client If the client were dumb — say, it just pinged a REST endpoint whenever it felt like it — two things break. First, *receiving* updates becomes impossible without polling every few seconds, which murders battery and gives you a stale map. Second, without client-side filtering (accuracy thresholds, displacement filters, background throttling), Redis GEO and Kafka get flooded with garbage: duplicate coordinates, 200m-accuracy indoor fixes, updates from phones sitting on a nightstand. The publisher tier and Redis shards take the hit first, then Kafka backs up, then every subscriber sees lag. ## The number The design assumes **3.3M location updates/sec** (100M concurrent users ÷ 30s). If the client published every 5s instead, that's 20M/sec — a 6× increase in Redis GEOADDs, Kafka throughput (~4 GB/s sustained), and fan-out deliveries (~400M/sec). The client's 30s timer is what makes the backend numbers tractable. ## The trade-off Pushing cadence and filtering into the client means the server sees "approximate nearby," not live motion — acceptable because a walking user only moves ~42m in 30s, well inside the 8km "nearby" radius.

lb.name: Connection Load Balancer
lb.summary: L4 load balancer holding millions of long-lived WebSocket flows; consistent-hashes on user_id.

sections.heading: Why L4
sections.body: WebSocket upgrades are sticky for the connection's lifetime — often hours. L4 with PROXY protocol preserves client IP for geo-bucketing analytics while keeping the LB out of the fast path.

sections.heading: Routing
sections.body: Consistent hash on user_id so a user lands on the same WebSocket server across reconnects. Minimises presence flap and keeps friend-subscription state warm per node.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- WS server dies → ~50K clients reconnect. LB spreads them across survivors; clients use jittered reconnect (1-10s) to avoid a thundering herd.
- Rolling deploy: graceful drain with SIGTERM signal; server sends CLOSE frames with `reconnect-after: Xs` hints.

bottlenecks.title: Reconnect storm exceeds LB handshake capacity
bottlenecks.trigger: An AZ or rack failure drops ~500K concurrent WebSocket flows (10 WS nodes × 50K). Clients reconnect within seconds; without jitter, the LB sees 100K+ TLS handshakes/sec against a steady-state of a few thousand. At 100M total concurrent connections, even a 1%/min flap = 16K new handshakes/sec sustained.
bottlenecks.symptom: LB CPU pegged on TLS termination, SYN queue overflows, new WS upgrades time out with 503s, clients stuck in 'Connecting...' loops, friend pins go grey globally.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Offload TLS to NLB + dedicated TLS terminators with session resumption (tickets) enabled; pre-warm LB capacity to 5x steady state; enforce server-sent `reconnect-after` hints with full jitter (1–30s) on graceful drain; SYN cookies on; rate-limit handshakes per source IP at the edge.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert when LB handshake QPS > 5× 1-hour baseline, TLS handshake p99 > 500ms, or SYN backlog drops > 0. Track `new_connections_per_sec` vs `established_connections` ratio per LB node.

bottlenecks.title: Consistent-hash ring reshuffle on WS node churn
bottlenecks.trigger: A WS node dies or is added during deploy. With 2000 WS nodes and naive consistent hashing, ~1/2000 of 100M = 50K users get remapped per node change; a rolling deploy of 100 nodes reshuffles 5M connections. Users land on cold nodes with no in-process subscription state.
bottlenecks.symptom: During deploys: latency spike on first location frame after reconnect (cold friend-list load), temporary duplicate deliveries as both old and new WS nodes briefly think they own the user, etcd routing table thrashing at >10K writes/sec.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use bounded-load consistent hashing (Google's algorithm, load factor 1.25) to cap churn; stagger rolling deploys to ≤10 nodes at a time with 60s settle windows; have WS nodes publish graceful-drain CLOSE frames with `reconnect-after: 5-30s` jitter; keep etcd TTL at 60s so stale routes self-expire.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: `connection_remap_rate` per deploy event; alert if >2% of total connections remap in a 1-min window. Track etcd write QPS on `/routes/*` — baseline ~1.6M/min (100M ÷ 60s TTL refresh); alert on 2× spikes.

bottlenecks.title: Per-LB-node flow table saturation at long-lived WS scale
bottlenecks.trigger: LB holds up to 1M concurrent flows per node (alternative spec). With 100M concurrent WebSockets system-wide, you need ≥100 LB nodes just for flow-table headroom. Each flow consumes ~10KB of conntrack state → 10GB RAM per million flows; TCP ephemeral port exhaustion on upstream side if LB NATs to WS (64K ports per (src,dst) pair).
bottlenecks.symptom: New connections fail with 'no route to host' or silently hang; conntrack table full errors in dmesg; existing connections fine but no new ones accepted on specific LB nodes; uneven load across LB fleet.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use Direct Server Return (DSR) or PROXY protocol to avoid NAT and port exhaustion; tune `nf_conntrack_max` to 4M+ per node; size LB fleet to 50% utilization of flow-table ceiling (cap at 500K flows/node for 1M-capable hardware); shard LB VIPs across multiple IPs to multiply ephemeral port space on upstream.
bottlenecks.detection: Metrics: `conntrack_entries / conntrack_max` per node (alert >70%), `ephemeral_port_utilization` upstream-side (alert >60%), per-LB connection count distribution (alert on stddev > 20% of mean indicating imbalance).

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a Load Balancer here Nearby Friends isn't a request/response app — it's 100 million phones holding **open WebSocket connections** to our servers at all times, each pushing GPS every 30 seconds and waiting for friends' updates to stream back. No single server can hold 100M sockets (kernel limits, memory, CPU), so we need ~2000 WebSocket servers and something in front to spread clients across them. That's the LB's job: accept the TLS handshake, pick a WS server, and then get out of the way for the hours-long life of that connection. The twist: because we want a user to land on the *same* WS server across reconnects (so their friend-subscription state stays warm in-process), the LB consistent-hashes on `user_id` instead of round-robin. This is specific to Nearby Friends — a stateless REST API wouldn't care where a request lands. ## What breaks without it Without an LB, clients would need to know a specific server's IP. When that server dies (taking 50K connections with it), every one of those users is stuck until someone ships a new app version. With the LB, those 50K clients reconnect, get hashed onto survivors, and are back on the map within seconds. ## The number At **100M concurrent connections / 50K per WS node = 2000 WS servers**, the LB is the only thing that can route a new connection to the right one of 2000 boxes in milliseconds — and keep routing consistently after node churn. The trade-off: the LB becomes a critical, stateful-ish layer that itself needs careful capacity planning for reconnect storms.

ws.name: WebSocket Server
ws.summary: Stateful WebSocket server maintaining ~50K concurrent connections per node; terminal for both publish and receive frames.

sections.heading: Per-connection state
sections.body: user_id, device_id, last_location, subscribed_friend_ids, heartbeat_deadline. Held in-process — NOT in Redis — to keep per-frame handling sub-millisecond.

sections.heading: Publish path
sections.body:
1. Receive LOC frame
2. Validate (lat in [-90,90], lng in [-180,180], ts within ±5 min)
3. Hand off to Location Publisher (in-proc call, then Kafka produce)

sections.heading: Receive path
sections.body: Subscription Manager wakes this node when a friend publishes. Node looks up which of its locally-connected users are subscribed to that publisher and pushes a FRIEND_LOC frame to each.

sections.heading: Why stateful
sections.body: Putting connection state in Redis would add a 1-2ms round trip to every single location frame. At 3.3M publishes/sec that's crippling. Stateful design keeps the hot path purely in-process.

lost: Topic-based pub/sub is awkward for friend-graph fan-out
Harder to attach per-connection app logic (auth, rate limit)

gained: Works through any proxy / corporate firewall
lost: New TCP/TLS handshake every poll → 10x battery
Presence is coarse — you only know a user is online when they poll

bottlenecks.title: Per-node connection ceiling at 50K long-lived WebSockets
bottlenecks.trigger: Each WS node holds ~50K concurrent connections to reach 100M total across 2000 nodes. Memory per connection (TLS buffers ~32KB + in-proc state: user_id, subscribed_friend_ids of ~200 entries, last_location) totals ~50-80KB → 2.5-4GB RAM just for connection state, plus kernel file-descriptor and epoll overhead. A viral event or 10% DAU spike pushes nodes toward 60K+ and triggers OOM or fd exhaustion.
bottlenecks.symptom: New WS upgrades fail with 'too many open files' or ECONNRESET; existing connections get slower send calls as epoll churns; node OOM-killed, dumping 50K users onto neighbors and triggering a cascade.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Hard cap at 50K connections/node with 503 + reconnect-after hint when exceeded; raise ulimit -n to 200K and tune net.core.somaxconn, tcp_mem; use epoll edge-triggered with per-connection write buffer cap of 16KB; autoscale WS fleet on connection_count/node_capacity > 0.75; use bounded-load consistent hashing (load factor 1.25) so LB refuses to overfill hot nodes.
bottlenecks.detection: Metrics: concurrent_connections per node (alert >40K = 80% of cap), open_fds/fd_limit ratio (alert >0.7), RSS memory (alert >80% of node), accept error rate. Page when any node crosses 45K for >2 min.

bottlenecks.title: Inbound publish + outbound fan-out CPU saturation
bottlenecks.trigger: Per node: 50K users × 1 publish/30s = 1.67K inbound LOC frames/sec, plus fan-out receive of ~33K FRIEND_LOC pushes/sec (fan-out ratio 20× / 2000 nodes × 66M total = 33K/node). Each frame costs protobuf decode, validation, in-proc map lookup, and TLS encrypt on send. At ~10µs/frame CPU budget per core, a 16-core node is already at 35K events/sec per core → headroom evaporates during reconnect storms or when fan-out spikes (e.g., events like New Year's Eve).
bottlenecks.symptom: send queue depth grows, WS frame delivery latency p99 jumps from 5ms to 500ms+, friends see pins lag 10-30s behind reality, server CPU pegged at 95%+, eventually heartbeat_deadline missed and clients disconnected en masse.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Offload TLS to kernel TLS (kTLS) or dedicated sidecar; batch outbound fan-out pushes per subscriber (coalesce multiple FRIEND_LOC frames in a 50ms window into one WS frame); use flatbuffers or pre-encoded protobuf to skip re-encoding on fan-out; pin WS goroutines/threads to cores with SO_REUSEPORT; drop oldest queued frame when per-connection send buffer > 16KB rather than blocking.
bottlenecks.detection: Metrics: frame_handle_latency_p99 per direction (alert >50ms), cpu_utilization per core (alert >80% sustained 1 min), send_queue_depth per connection (alert if p99 > 100 frames), dropped_frames counter, event_loop_lag.

bottlenecks.title: In-process subscription state lost on node failure / deploy
bottlenecks.trigger: Per-connection state (user_id, subscribed_friend_ids of ~200 entries, last_location) is held in-process for sub-ms latency. A node crash drops 50K users' state instantly; a rolling deploy of 100 nodes wipes 5M users' warm state. Each reconnect triggers a fresh friends_svc.friends_of Cassandra fetch → 50K × 180 rows = 9M row reads in seconds, hammering the Friends Service.
bottlenecks.symptom: After any WS node loss: Friends Service QPS spikes 100× baseline, Cassandra p99 latency climbs, cache miss storm on subscribers_of cache, first FRIEND_LOC frame after reconnect delayed 2-10s, users see grey pins globally during deploys.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Warm-resume cookies: on graceful close, WS sends client a signed state blob (friend_ids + last_seq); client replays on reconnect, skipping DB fetch; stagger rolling deploys to ≤10 nodes with 60s settle windows; pre-fetch subscriber list into a shared Redis L2 cache with 5-min TTL as fallback; use bounded-load consistent hashing so reconnects mostly land on the same node the user was on.
bottlenecks.detection: Metrics: friends_svc_qps_spike_ratio (alert >5× baseline in 1 min), time_to_first_frame after reconnect (alert p95 >3s), cold_connection_rate (new conn with no client-provided state cookie), Cassandra read latency p99 on edges table.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a WebSocket Server for Nearby Friends Nearby Friends is fundamentally a **push** problem, not a pull problem. Your phone needs to *send* its GPS every 30 seconds, and — more importantly — your phone needs to *receive* a friend's new location the moment it lands, without asking. A regular HTTP request/response server can't do the second half: the server has no way to wake up your phone and say "Alice just moved." WebSockets give us a single long-lived connection where both sides can send frames at any time, which is exactly the shape of this traffic. ## What breaks without it If we used plain HTTP polling instead, every client would have to ask "any friend updates?" every few seconds. At 100M concurrent users polling every 5s, that's 20M requests/sec of mostly-empty responses, each paying the cost of a TCP+TLS handshake. Battery dies, the API tier melts, and users still see friend pins that are 5–10 seconds stale. The operator sees a CPU graph that looks like a wall; the user sees a spinner and a dead phone. ## The number The design targets **100M concurrent connections across ~2000 WS nodes = 50K connections per node**. Each node holds per-connection state (user_id, subscribed friends, last location) purely in-process, so handling an incoming LOC frame is a hashmap lookup instead of a Redis round-trip. At 3.3M publishes/sec across the fleet, saving even 1ms per frame on state lookup is the difference between 2000 nodes and 20,000. ## The trade-off Keeping connection state in-process means a dying WS node drops 50K users who must reconnect and reload their friend subscriptions — we accept that blast radius to keep the hot path sub-millisecond.

pub.name: Location Publisher
pub.summary: Co-located with the WebSocket server; writes each location to Redis GEO and emits to Kafka for fan-out.

sections.heading: Two writes, one trigger
sections.body:
1. `GEOADD locations <lng> <lat> <user_id>` → Redis GEO (authoritative current location, queryable by radius)
2. Produce to Kafka topic `locations` partitioned by user_id → feeds Subscription Manager for fan-out

sections.heading: Why both
sections.body: Redis GEO answers 'which friends are within 5 miles of me right now?' (radius query). Kafka drives 'push my friends' clients this new location' (fan-out). Trying to serve both from Redis alone would require scan-all-followers on every publish.

sections.heading: Batching
sections.body: The publisher batches Kafka produces in 10ms windows (linger.ms=10) — amortises the produce overhead without hurting end-to-end latency since WS → screen budget is 1-2 seconds anyway.

bottlenecks.title: Dual-write divergence between Redis GEO and Kafka
bottlenecks.trigger: Publisher issues two async writes per LOC frame at 3.3M publishes/sec. If Redis GEOADD succeeds but Kafka produce fails (or vice versa), fan-out and radius queries diverge. At 0.01% partial-failure rate that's 330 divergent writes/sec, or ~28M/day where Redis shows a user at location X but subscribers were never pushed.
bottlenecks.symptom: Users open the Nearby tab and see a friend pinned at location A (from GEOSEARCH), while that friend's live feed keeps showing location B from an older push — or vice versa, 'ghost' pins that never update until the next successful publish.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Write to Kafka first with acks=1, then derive the Redis GEOADD from a Kafka consumer (single source of truth), OR use a transactional outbox: stage both writes in a local buffer, commit to Kafka, and have a separate consumer apply to Redis idempotently keyed by (user_id, ts). Add a reconciliation job that re-GEOADDs from Kafka offsets every 60s.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: divergence_rate = |redis_geo_writes - kafka_produces| / total_publishes per 1-min window; alert if >0.05%. Also track per-publisher last_redis_ts vs last_kafka_ts skew; page if p99 skew > 5s.

bottlenecks.title: Kafka producer backpressure stalls the WS hot path
bottlenecks.trigger: Publisher is co-located with WS and called in-proc per LOC frame. At 3.3M produces/sec with linger.ms=10 and batch.size=64KB, any Kafka broker slowdown (GC pause, ISR shrink, partition leader election across 1024 partitions) causes producer buffer (default 32MB) to fill in ~1-2s. When buffer.memory is exhausted, send blocks — directly stalling the WS receive loop.
bottlenecks.symptom: WS frame_handle_latency_p99 jumps from 5ms to seconds; client send queues back up; heartbeat deadlines missed; 50K connections per node start dropping; cascade to neighbor nodes as reconnects flood.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Set max.block.ms=0 so send fails fast rather than blocking; on producer-queue-full, fall back to direct Redis-only write + local disk spool (replayed by sidecar into Kafka when recovered); increase buffer.memory to 128MB and compression.type=lz4; shard producers (one per CPU core) with SO_REUSEPORT; monitor and pre-emptively shed 1% of publishes when buffer > 70% full.
bottlenecks.detection: Metrics: kafka_producer_buffer_available_bytes (alert <30% of buffer.memory), record_send_rate vs record_queue_time_avg (alert if queue_time > 50ms), producer.send_blocked_ms per second (alert >100ms/s). Page on any sustained buffer >80% for 30s.

bottlenecks.title: Redis GEO shard hotspotting on geographically clustered publishers
bottlenecks.trigger: Sharding is by user_id % 20, which balances writes across shards uniformly — BUT a single shard still sees 3.3M/20 = 165K GEOADDs/sec. Redis single-threaded command processing caps around 100-150K ops/sec per instance before CPU saturation; any shard running hot (e.g., due to rebalance, AOF rewrite, or a noisy pipelined client) becomes the publisher tier's latency ceiling.
bottlenecks.symptom: Publisher p99 latency spikes from 3ms to 20-50ms on one shard; tail latency propagates into WS frame handling; GEOADD timeouts cause retries, doubling effective load on the hot shard and risking full unavailability of that 5M-user slice.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Increase shard count from 20 to 64+ (target <60K ops/sec per shard for headroom); use Redis Cluster with pipelining batched per-shard (amortize RTT); disable AOF or use appendfsync=no for GEO-only shards (Kafka is durable backbone); deploy Redis 7+ with I/O threads to push single-instance ceiling to ~250K ops/sec; add circuit breaker on Publisher that skips GEOADD (keeps Kafka path alive) when shard p99 > 20ms.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-shard metrics: redis_commands_processed_per_sec (alert >120K), redis_cpu_sys+user (alert >70%), GEOADD latency p99 per shard (alert >10ms), shard load stddev across the 20 shards (alert if max/mean > 1.5x indicating imbalance).

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Location Publisher exists here For Nearby Friends, every location update has to do *two completely different jobs*. First, it needs to become the answer to "who's within 5 miles of me right now?" — a spatial query. Second, it needs to wake up the ~20 friends who've opted in to see this user and push the update to their phones — a fan-out. These are fundamentally different access patterns, and no single storage system does both well. The Publisher is the small piece of code that sits right after the WebSocket server and splits each incoming location into the right shape for each downstream system: a `GEOADD` into Redis (for radius queries) and a Kafka produce (for fan-out). ## What breaks without it If you tried to serve both needs from Redis alone, every publish would have to scan the publisher's follower list and push to each one — turning a sub-millisecond `GEOADD` into a multi-millisecond loop. Worse, Redis isn't durable or replayable, so a momentary Subscription Manager outage would silently drop updates. Users would see friend pins freeze; the operator would see Redis CPU pegged and no obvious recovery path. ## The number At **3.3M publishes/sec**, a single extra millisecond per publish means 3,300 CPU-seconds of work every wall-clock second — you'd need thousands more cores just to absorb it. The Publisher's dual-write keeps each path O(1): one `GEOADD` (~100µs) plus one batched Kafka produce (linger.ms=10 amortizes ~100 records per syscall). ## The trade-off Writing to two systems means they can briefly disagree — the designer accepts that eventual-consistency window in exchange for keeping both the radius query and the fan-out on their fastest respective paths.

geo.name: Redis GEO
geo.summary: Sharded Redis cluster using GEO commands (sorted sets with geohash scores) to store every active user's current location.

sections.heading: Data model
sections.body:
```
KEY locations:{shard_id}
TYPE GEO (sorted set with 52-bit interleaved geohash score)
MEMBER user_id → (lng, lat)
```
Shard by `user_id % 20`. Each shard holds ~5M members at ~500MB.

sections.heading: Query patterns
sections.body:
- `GEOADD locations 122.4194 37.7749 user_42` (write, O(log N))
- `GEOSEARCH locations FROMMEMBER user_42 BYRADIUS 5 mi ASC` (read, O(N+log M)) for the 'who is near me' query
- TTL not used — publisher explicitly `GEODEL`s on logout; otherwise stale entries age out via the user-level inactivity sweep.

sections.heading: Why Redis GEO not PostGIS
sections.body: PostGIS is a full spatial DB but at 3.3M writes/s each write is a multi-ms SQL transaction. Redis GEO is in-memory, lock-free, and GEOADD is ~100µs. The tradeoff is no complex polygon queries — but Nearby Friends only needs radius search.

gained: Uniform hex cells — no geohash stretching near poles
lost: Custom code instead of a built-in GEO command
Harder radius search — you have to compute ring of hexes
Won't sustain 3.3M QPS on any reasonable hardware

bottlenecks.title: Single-shard write saturation at 165K GEOADD/sec
bottlenecks.trigger: Sharding user_id % 20 spreads 3.3M publishes/sec evenly → 165K GEOADD/sec per shard. Redis is single-threaded on command execution and tops out at ~100–150K ops/sec per instance before CPU saturation; any AOF rewrite, BGSAVE, or slow SLOWLOG entry tips a shard over.
bottlenecks.symptom: GEOADD p99 climbs from <1ms to 20–50ms on one shard; Publisher backpressure propagates into the WS hot path; frame_handle_latency p99 spikes; 5M users (1/20 of traffic) see stale pins.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Increase shard count from 20 to 64+ (target <60K ops/sec/shard); enable Redis 7 I/O threads (io-threads 4) to push single-instance ceiling to ~250K ops/sec; pipeline GEOADDs per-shard from the Publisher to amortize RTT; disable AOF (appendonly no) — Kafka is the durable backbone; add a Publisher circuit breaker that skips GEOADD when shard p99 > 20ms.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-shard metrics: redis_commands_processed_total rate (alert >120K/sec), used_cpu_sys+user (alert >70%), GEOADD command latency p99 (alert >10ms), shard ops_per_sec stddev across 20 shards (alert if max/mean > 1.5× indicating hotspot).

bottlenecks.title: GEOSEARCH in dense urban cells returns 40K+ members per shard
bottlenecks.trigger: In SF/NYC/Tokyo, a 5-mile radius contains ~40K active users. GEOSEARCH is O(N+log M) where N is members in the bounding box; the query fans out to all 20 shards and each returns ~2K members. At open-tab QPS of even 100K/sec (0.1% of 100M concurrent), that's 2M per-shard GEOSEARCHes/sec with multi-KB reply payloads.
bottlenecks.symptom: Nearby tab open latency spikes from ~50ms to 500ms+ in dense cities; Redis output buffers grow, network egress on GEO shards pegs 10GbE; GEOADD latency collapses on the same shards due to single-threaded head-of-line blocking behind long GEOSEARCH replies.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Always GEOSEARCH with COUNT 1000 ASC (already specified) AND pre-intersect with the friend list — push `GEOSEARCH... FROMLONLAT... WITHCOORD` only for the ~180 friend_ids via pipelined GEOPOS + client-side distance filter; OR maintain a per-user 'friend geo index' keyed by user_id holding only that user's friends' coords, trading memory for bounded query cost; cap client-visible radius to 8km and zoom-dependent COUNT.
bottlenecks.detection: Metrics: GEOSEARCH result cardinality histogram (alert p99 > 5000), GEOSEARCH latency p99 per shard (alert >30ms), client_output_buffer_length on GEO shards (alert >10MB), network_bytes_out per shard (alert >70% of NIC).

bottlenecks.title: Shard failover loses current locations for 5M users
bottlenecks.trigger: Redis GEO is in-memory with AOF likely disabled (for write perf). A single shard failover (OOM, node reboot, AZ blip) drops ~5M users' current coordinates. Replica promotion recovers the sorted set only up to last replication offset, typically lagging 100s–1000s of GEOADDs behind.
bottlenecks.symptom: After shard failover: GEOSEARCH returns empty or stale results for 5% of users (1/20 of the base); Nearby tab shows 'no friends nearby' for affected users until their next 30s publish; up to 30s window of degraded radius queries globally, coinciding with reconnect storm.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Run a Redis-side consumer of the Kafka `locations` topic as a warm-standby hydrator — on failover, replay last 60s of Kafka into the promoted replica before accepting reads (Kafka retention is 1h, plenty); use Redis Cluster with replica-per-shard and min-replicas-to-write=1; on Publisher, aggressively retry GEOADD against the new primary using the Kafka record as source of truth.
bottlenecks.detection: Metrics: redis_master_link_status per shard, replication_offset_lag (alert >10K commands), post-failover GEOSEARCH empty_result_rate (alert >2% for any shard), time_since_last_geoadd per user_id sampled (alert p99 > 90s indicating lost writes).

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Redis GEO is here Nearby Friends has two very different read patterns. One is "push my latest location to my ~20 friends" — that's what Kafka and the Subscription Manager handle. The other is "when I open the app, show me every friend within 5 miles of where I'm standing right now." That second query needs a **spatial index**: something that can take a point and a radius and return the members inside it, fast. Redis GEO is exactly that — a sorted set where each member's score is a geohash, so a radius search becomes a bounded range scan instead of comparing distances to 100M users one by one. ## What breaks without it Without a spatial index, answering "who's within 5 miles of me?" would mean scanning every active user's coordinates and computing Haversine distances — hundreds of millions of comparisons per query. The user would tap the Nearby tab and stare at a spinner for seconds; the operator would watch CPU melt on whatever service tried to do the scan. You could push this into Postgres/PostGIS, but then you'd pay ~10–40ms per write on a workload that does 3.3M writes/sec — that service would simply not keep up. ## The number At **3.3M location updates/sec**, each publish has to finish its write in well under a millisecond to not back up the publisher tier. Redis GEOADD is ~100µs because it's in-memory and single-threaded per shard; sharded 20 ways, each shard absorbs ~165K writes/sec comfortably. PostGIS at ~20ms/write would need >60,000 parallel connections to match — not viable. ## The trade-off In exchange for this speed, Redis GEO only does radius/box queries — no polygons, no routing, no "inside this neighborhood shape." Nearby Friends only ever needs radius, so that limitation costs nothing here.

kafka.name: Location Stream (Kafka)
kafka.summary: Partitioned log of all location updates; decouples publishers from subscription fan-out.

sections.heading: Topic design
sections.body: Topic `locations`, partitioned by `user_id` (hashed) → 1024 partitions. Retention 1 hour (fan-out is near-real-time; we don't replay history).

sections.heading: Producer config
sections.body: `acks=1` (leader-only) — we trade durability for latency since Redis GEO is the system of record anyway. `linger.ms=10` and `batch.size=64KB` give ~10x compression of small records.

sections.heading: Consumer
sections.body: Subscription Manager consumes all partitions with a consumer group of ~200 workers. Each record triggers a friend-graph lookup and fan-out to WS servers.

gained: Already have Redis in the stack
lost: No tiered storage — 1h retention costs RAM

bottlenecks.title: Partition leader hotspotting at 3.3M msg/sec across 1024 partitions
bottlenecks.trigger: Topic `locations` with 1024 partitions absorbing 3.3M publishes/sec averages ~3.2K msg/sec per partition, but key=user_id hashing plus active-user skew (e.g. a celebrity or a region waking up) pushes some partition leaders to 20-50K msg/sec. With 660 MB/s sustained and 2 GB/s peak, a single overloaded broker leader handling 10+ hot partitions saturates its NIC (10GbE ≈ 1.25 GB/s) or page cache.
bottlenecks.symptom: Produce latency p99 jumps from ~5ms to 200ms+ on specific partitions; Subscription Manager consumer lag climbs on the same partitions; friend pins lag 10-30s behind reality for users whose publishers hash to hot partitions; ISR shrinks and under-replicated-partitions alerts fire.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Increase partition count to 4096 for finer leader distribution; use sticky partitioner with key=user_id but rebalance leaders across brokers via `kafka-reassign-partitions` weekly; enable rack-aware leader election; set `num.replica.fetchers=8` and `replica.fetch.max.bytes=16MB`; deploy at least 30 brokers so no broker leads >35 partitions; monitor and auto-rebalance with Cruise Control.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-partition metrics: `MessagesInPerSec` stddev across 1024 partitions (alert if max/mean > 5×); `UnderReplicatedPartitions` > 0; per-broker `BytesOutPerSec` (alert >70% of NIC); produce request p99 latency per partition (alert >50ms).

bottlenecks.title: Consumer group rebalance stalls fan-out at 200 workers × 1024 partitions
bottlenecks.trigger: Subscription Manager runs a consumer group of ~200 workers across 1024 partitions (~5 partitions/worker). Any worker restart, deploy, or network blip triggers a group rebalance; with eager rebalancing, ALL 200 workers stop consuming during reassignment. At 3.3M msg/sec, a 10-second rebalance builds a 33M-message backlog — 66M fan-out deliveries delayed.
bottlenecks.symptom: Brief but total fan-out outage during any sub deploy: friend pins freeze globally for 10-30s, consumer lag spikes to tens of millions, then drains over 1-2 minutes causing a thundering burst of FRIEND_LOC frames to WS servers (potentially overwhelming them).
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use cooperative-sticky assignor (`partition.assignment.strategy=CooperativeStickyAssignor`) so only moving partitions pause; set `session.timeout.ms=10000` and `heartbeat.interval.ms=3000`; use static group membership (`group.instance.id`) to survive pod restarts without rebalance; roll deploys with `max-unavailable=1` and 30s settle window; pre-warm new workers before removing old.
bottlenecks.detection: Metrics: `kafka.consumer.rebalance.rate` (alert on any rebalance outside maintenance window); `records-lag-max` per worker (alert >100K); `rebalance-latency-max` (alert >2s); count of active consumers in group vs expected 200.

bottlenecks.title: 1-hour retention at 660 MB/s peaks to 7.2 TB of broker disk + page cache pressure
bottlenecks.trigger: Retention of 1 hour × 660 MB/s sustained = ~2.4 TB; at 2 GB/s peak = ~7.2 TB. Replicated ×3 = 7-22 TB of disk across the cluster. Page cache must hold the hot tail (~last few minutes) for consumers to read without disk I/O; any consumer lag beyond page cache (e.g. after a rebalance) forces disk reads and crushes producer throughput on the same brokers.
bottlenecks.symptom: After a consumer lag event, broker disk read IOPS spike, produce latency p99 doubles, page cache hit ratio drops below 95%, producers see `RequestTimedOutException`, and a feedback loop forms where lagging consumers slow producers, which slows WS publish ACKs, which pushes clients to reconnect.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use NVMe SSDs (sustained 3 GB/s read) on brokers; size RAM to hold 10 min of hot tail (~400 GB per broker with 30 brokers); enable tiered storage (Kafka 3.6+ `remote.storage.enable=true`) to offload older segments to S3; reduce retention to 15 min (fan-out is near-real-time, no replay needed); set `log.segment.bytes=512MB` for faster segment roll; compression=lz4 already reduces footprint ~3×.
bottlenecks.detection: Broker metrics: `LogEndOffset - LogStartOffset` disk usage per partition; page cache hit ratio via `node_exporter` (alert <95%); disk read IOPS (alert if non-zero sustained — indicates reading from disk not cache); `RemoteLogManager` fetch rate if tiered storage enabled.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Kafka sits in the middle of Nearby Friends The Location Publisher has already done two things with every GPS update: written it to Redis GEO (for "who's near me?" queries) and handed it off to Kafka. The Kafka part exists because of a mismatch in speed and shape. Publishers produce 3.3M location updates per second in a steady firehose. Subscribers — the Subscription Manager workers that figure out whose friends need to be notified — do a much heavier job per message (friend-graph lookup, then push to ~20 WS servers). If publishers called the fan-out code directly, any hiccup downstream (a slow Cassandra read, a WS node restart) would back up into the WebSocket hot path and make *publishing* slow. Kafka is the shock absorber: publishers dump updates and walk away; consumers drain at their own pace. ## What breaks without it Without Kafka, the Publisher would have to synchronously loop over 20 subscribers per update and push to each. A 50ms blip on one WS server stalls that whole publish, which stalls the WebSocket's receive loop, which makes the client think the server is dead. The user sees their own location stop updating; the operator sees WS CPU pegged on blocked threads and a cascade of reconnects. The 3.3M/sec publish rate becomes coupled to the 66M/sec delivery rate, and the whole system fails together. ## The number 3.3M publishes/sec × ~20 subscribers each = **66M fan-out deliveries/sec**. Kafka's 1024 partitions let ~200 consumer workers parallelize that work independently of how fast publishers are writing. ## The trade-off You accept a small added latency (tens of ms of queueing) to decouple two tiers running at very different speeds.

sub.name: Subscription Manager
sub.summary: Consumes location stream, looks up each publisher's subscribers, and fans out to the WS server hosting each subscriber.

sections.heading: Core loop
Fan-out math
sections.body: Average 20 active subscribers per publisher → 3.3M * 20 = 66M push events/sec. Each is ~100 bytes → 6.6 GB/s aggregate inter-service traffic.

sections.heading: Routing table
sections.body: Every WS server registers its user_id → server_id binding in a shared etcd / ZK path on connect. Subscription Manager keeps a hot cache refreshed via watch. On stale-cache miss (5xx from push), record is NACKed and retried on next flush.

lost: Heavier ops — requires checkpoint storage, job manager

bottlenecks.title: Routing-table lookup storm against etcd at 66M fan-out/sec
bottlenecks.trigger: Each of 3.3M location records/sec requires ~20 routing.lookup(sub_id) calls to find the WS host for each subscriber — 66M lookups/sec. A cold cache (after Subscription Manager deploy or etcd watch reset) or a WS deploy that invalidates 5M sub_id→host bindings forces those lookups through to etcd, which tops out around 10K reads/sec per node.
bottlenecks.symptom: Fan-out latency p99 jumps from ~10ms to seconds; Kafka consumer lag climbs across all 200 workers simultaneously; etcd leader CPU pegged, watch events delayed, and 5xx NACKs on push spike because workers route to stale hosts.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Keep routing table fully in-process on every Subscription Manager worker, hydrated by a single etcd watch stream (not per-lookup reads); fall back to a Redis L2 mirror of /routes/* with 60s TTL; batch push RPCs per destination WS host so one host lookup covers N subscribers; on push 5xx, refresh just the affected key rather than the whole table.
bottlenecks.detection: Metrics: routing_cache_hit_ratio (alert <99.5%), etcd_read_qps from sub workers (alert >50K/sec aggregate), push_nack_rate due to wrong_host (alert >0.1%), routing_table_staleness_seconds (alert p99 >5s).

bottlenecks.title: subscribers_of cache miss storm against Friends Service
bottlenecks.trigger: Worst-case 2B (publisher, subscriber) tuples; design caches only the active ~20M publishers with 60s TTL. At 3.3M publishes/sec, even a 1% miss rate = 33K Cassandra queries/sec against subscribers_of; a full cache cold-start (worker deploy, Kafka rebalance, or diurnal active-set shift) produces a brief burst of hundreds of thousands of reads/sec across the 200 workers, each pulling ~20-row partitions.
bottlenecks.symptom: Friends Service p99 spikes from ~5ms to 100ms+; Cassandra read latency climbs and coordinator timeouts appear; Subscription Manager consumer lag grows on all partitions; friend pins lag 10–30s behind reality until the cache rewarms.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use a shared Redis L2 cache for subscribers_of with longer TTL (5 min) as a second layer in front of Cassandra; on edge mutation, invalidate both L1 and L2; stagger worker deploys ≤10% at a time so in-process caches don't all cold-start together; pre-warm by scanning the active-publishers set on worker startup; rate-limit Cassandra reads per worker and fall back to last-known subscriber list on timeout.
bottlenecks.detection: Metrics: subscribers_of_cache_hit_ratio per worker (alert <98%), friends_svc_qps (alert >100K/sec aggregate), cassandra_read_latency_p99 (alert >20ms), consumer_lag correlated with cache_miss_rate.

bottlenecks.title: Per-worker fan-out CPU and RPC-concurrency limit
bottlenecks.trigger: 200 workers split 66M push/sec = 330K RPCs/sec per worker. Each involves a routing lookup, gRPC serialize, TLS send, and response handling — realistically 5–20ms of wall time under contention. Publish spikes (New Year's, sports events, celebrity movement) or hot partitions push certain workers to 2–5× baseline, exhausting thread pools and gRPC channel concurrency caps.
bottlenecks.symptom: Handful of Subscription Manager workers show Kafka consumer lag while others stay caught up; fan-out latency p99 bimodal (fast path ~10ms, slow path ~500ms); gRPC channel queue depth alerts on specific WS hosts; friend pins freeze for a subset of users whose publishers hash to lagging workers.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Coalesce multiple pushes to the same WS host into a single batched gRPC call (one network round-trip per WS host per 50ms window, not per subscriber); raise worker count to 400+ to halve per-worker load; use HTTP/2 multiplexing with ≥1000 concurrent streams per WS host; shed oldest pending pushes when per-worker queue > 10K; autoscale on consumer_lag, not CPU.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-worker metrics: kafka_consumer_lag (alert >50K records), fanout_rpc_queue_depth (alert >5K), fanout_latency_p99 (alert >100ms), worker_cpu (alert >75%), stddev of lag across 200 workers (alert if max/mean > 3×).

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Subscription Manager exists for Nearby Friends When Alice publishes her GPS coordinates, *someone* has to figure out which of her friends opted in to see her location and push the update to each of their phones. That's a graph traversal plus a routing decision plus ~20 network calls — far too much work to do inside the WebSocket server's hot path, which is already busy handling 50,000 live connections and 1,600+ location frames per second. The Subscription Manager is the dedicated worker tier that drains Kafka, asks the Friends Service "who subscribes to Alice?", looks up which WS server each subscriber is connected to, and fires the pushes. It exists precisely because fan-out is the heaviest step in the whole pipeline and needs to scale independently from publishing. ## What breaks without it If the WS server tried to do fan-out inline, a single slow friend-graph lookup or a sluggish peer WS node would block Alice's next location publish. Her own map pin would stop updating for her friends; operators would see WebSocket receive queues backing up and CPU pegged on blocked I/O. Worse, a downstream hiccup in one region would cascade into publish latency *everywhere*, because publishers and fan-out would be tightly coupled. ## The number Fan-out is **3.3M publishes/sec × ~20 subscribers = 66M delivery events/sec**. Split across ~200 Kafka consumer workers, that's ~330K pushes/sec per worker — tractable only because this tier is dedicated to fan-out and nothing else. ## The trade-off Decoupling adds a small queueing delay (tens of ms) to friend updates — acceptable when the UI budget is 1–2 seconds end-to-end.

friends.name: Friends Service
friends.summary: Stores the friend graph and the 'nearby sharing' opt-in flag per edge.

sections.heading: Data model
sections.body:
```
TABLE edges owner_id BIGINT friend_id BIGINT nearby_share BOOLEAN created_at TIMESTAMP PRIMARY KEY ((owner_id), friend_id) TABLE subscribers_of // inverted index friend_id BIGINT subscriber_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY ((friend_id), subscriber_id)
```

sections.heading: Why two tables
sections.body: We need both forward (my friends) and reverse (who shares with me) lookups in O(1). Writing both at edge-mutation time (double write) is the standard denormalisation for read-heavy graphs.

sections.heading: Caching
sections.body: Subscription Manager pins a per-publisher subscriber list in-process with a 60s TTL. At 20 subscribers * 100M publishers = 2B tuples worst-case — in practice we only cache the active ~20M publishers → manageable.

bottlenecks.title: subscribers_of hot-partition read storm at fan-out scale
bottlenecks.trigger: Subscription Manager resolves subscribers for every one of 3.3M publishes/sec. With a 60s in-proc TTL and ~20M active publishers cached, even a 1% miss rate = 33K Cassandra reads/sec; a cold start of 200 sub workers (deploy, rebalance) can burst to 100K+ reads/sec. Celebrity/influencer rows with 10K+ subscribers create wide-partition hotspots on `subscribers_of` keyed by friend_id.
bottlenecks.symptom: p99 read latency on `subscribers_of` climbs from ~5ms to 100ms+; Subscription Manager consumer lag grows on specific Kafka partitions; friend pins lag 10–30s globally during deploys; Cassandra coordinator timeouts and tombstone warnings for high-degree friend_ids.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add a shared Redis L2 cache in front of Cassandra with 5-min TTL keyed by friend_id; cap wide partitions by bucketing high-degree nodes (friend_id, bucket) with bucket = subscriber_id % 16; stagger sub-worker deploys to ≤10% at a time to avoid synchronized cold starts; pre-warm L1 from the active-publishers set on worker start; set Cassandra read_repair_chance=0 and use LOCAL_ONE consistency for this read path.
bottlenecks.detection: Metrics: subscribers_of_cache_hit_ratio per sub worker (alert <98%), friends_svc read QPS (alert >100K/sec aggregate), Cassandra read latency p99 per table (alert >20ms), partition_size_bytes histogram on subscribers_of (alert on any partition >100MB), tombstone_scanned_histogram (alert p99 >1000).

bottlenecks.title: Dual-write inconsistency between edges and subscribers_of on edge mutation
bottlenecks.trigger: Every friend add / nearby_share toggle writes to both `edges` (forward) and `subscribers_of` (reverse). Cassandra has no cross-partition transactions; a failure between the two writes leaves the graph asymmetric. At ~1000 edge mutations/sec across 1B users, even 0.1% partial failures = ~1/sec divergent edges, accumulating to 86K/day of ghost or missing subscriptions.
bottlenecks.symptom: Users toggle off 'share my location' but friends keep seeing their pin (reverse index stale); or users add a friend who opts in, but the subscriber never receives FRIEND_LOC pushes because `subscribers_of` was never updated; user-reported privacy bugs that are hard to reproduce.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Write mutations to a durable outbox (Kafka topic `edge-mutations` with acks=all) first, then have an idempotent consumer apply both table writes keyed by (owner_id, friend_id, version); add a nightly reconciliation job scanning edges vs subscribers_of with Merkle-tree diff; on toggle-off, treat subscribers_of as advisory and have the Publisher re-check edges.nearby_share on a sampled basis.
bottlenecks.detection: Metrics: dual_write_partial_failure_count (alert >10/min), reconciliation_divergence_count (alert >1000/day), privacy_toggle_latency_to_effect p99 (alert >60s), background diff job output diff rows per day.

bottlenecks.title: 2B reverse-index tuples dominate storage and compaction I/O
bottlenecks.trigger: Worst-case 1B users × avg 200 friends = 200B edges; subscribers_of mirrors this at ~2B active (nearby_share=true, 10% opt-in) tuples, replicated RF=3. At ~80 bytes/row overhead on Cassandra, that's ~500GB–1TB logical × 3 = 1.5–3TB plus compaction overhead. High-degree partitions (celebrities with 1M followers) blow past Cassandra's 100MB recommended partition size.
bottlenecks.symptom: Compaction falls behind on nodes holding celebrity partitions; read latency p99 becomes bimodal (fast for normal users, 100ms+ for high-degree friend_ids); disk space alerts during compaction as SSTables temporarily double; repair operations take days.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use LeveledCompactionStrategy for read-heavy subscribers_of; bucket high-degree partitions as (friend_id, bucket_id) with sub_id % 16 buckets so no partition exceeds ~60K rows; set gc_grace_seconds=1 day to bound tombstone accumulation for opt-out churn; use TWCS only if TTL-based retention is added; provision 3× peak logical size on disk to absorb compaction.
bottlenecks.detection: Metrics: partition_size_histogram per table (alert any partition >50MB), pending_compactions per node (alert >100 sustained), disk_used_ratio (alert >65%), SSTables_per_read p99 (alert >4), repair_duration per keyspace.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Friends Service is here Nearby Friends is fundamentally a **filtered** location system: Alice doesn't broadcast her GPS to the world, only to the subset of her friends who have explicitly toggled on "share my location." That filter — the social graph plus the per-edge opt-in flag — has to live somewhere authoritative. The Friends Service is that somewhere. Every time Alice publishes a location, *something* needs to answer "who opted in to see Alice?" in milliseconds, and every time Bob opens the Nearby tab, *something* needs to answer "who are Bob's friends?" just as fast. Without a dedicated service owning this graph, there's no single place to enforce privacy correctly. ## What breaks without it If the friend graph were baked into the WebSocket servers or Redis, a user toggling "stop sharing" would take minutes or hours to propagate — and during that window their ex-friend would keep seeing their pin move. The operator would see privacy bug reports pile up with no good way to reproduce them; the fan-out tier would keep happily pushing locations to subscribers who shouldn't receive them. ## The number Fan-out is **3.3M publishes/sec × ~20 subscribers = 66M deliveries/sec**. Every one of those 3.3M publishes needs a `subscribers_of(publisher)` lookup. That's why the service maintains a *reverse index* (`subscribers_of`) alongside the forward one — looking up 20 subscribers per publish has to be O(1), not a scan of 200 friends to check each one's opt-in bit. ## The trade-off Denormalizing into two tables means every edge mutation is a dual-write that can briefly disagree — accepted in exchange for O(1) reads on the hot path.

notif.name: Notification Service
notif.summary: Sends APNs/FCM pushes when a friend comes within N meters for the first time today ('Alice is now nearby').

sections.heading: When to push
sections.body: Consumes the same Kafka stream. For each location update, checks Redis GEO for friends within 500m and sends a push if (a) the subscriber is offline on WS and (b) we haven't notified for this friend pair in the last 6 hours.

sections.heading: Rate limiting
sections.body: Per-recipient token bucket. A user at a concert with 50 nearby friends should get ONE aggregated push, not 50.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- APNs throttling → exponential backoff; dropped notifications are acceptable (not critical path).
- Dead token → mark device invalid after 5 consecutive failures.

bottlenecks.title: APNs/FCM per-connection throughput ceiling vs 66M fan-out firehose
bottlenecks.trigger: Notifier consumes the same 3.3M location events/sec that drive fan-out. Even after filtering to offline subscribers with friends inside 500m (say 1-5% of events), that's still 30-150K candidate pushes/sec. APNs HTTP/2 caps at ~1000 concurrent streams per connection and ~10K pushes/sec per connection in practice; FCM similar. A single notifier worker pool with insufficient provider connections becomes the funnel.
bottlenecks.symptom: APNs returns 429 TooManyRequests / GOAWAY frames; notification delivery lag grows from seconds to minutes; 'Alice is now nearby' pushes arrive after Alice has already left; Kafka consumer lag on the notifier consumer group climbs while fan-out (sub manager) stays caught up.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Maintain a pool of ≥50 persistent HTTP/2 connections to APNs and ≥50 to FCM per notifier instance; shard by device_token hash; pre-filter in Kafka consumer BEFORE provider call (drop events where no subscriber is offline or no one within 500m) to cut 95%+ of work; use a separate low-priority Kafka topic for notifications so fan-out isn't coupled; set APNs `apns-priority: 5` (not 10) for nearby alerts to let Apple coalesce.
bottlenecks.detection: Metrics: apns_http2_stream_utilization per connection (alert >80%), apns_429_rate (alert >0.1%), notifier_kafka_consumer_lag (alert >100K records), p99 event_to_push_latency (alert >30s), GOAWAY frame count per minute.

bottlenecks.title: Per-recipient rate-limit state storage at 200M DAU
bottlenecks.trigger: Rate limit is 'at most 1 push per (recipient, friend) pair per 6 hours'. Worst case: 200M DAU × 200 friends × 10% opt-in = 4B active pairs, each needing a last-notified timestamp. At ~40 bytes/entry that's ~160GB of state. Token-bucket checks happen on every candidate event (tens of thousands/sec), so the store must be sub-ms read+write.
bottlenecks.symptom: If using Redis: memory pressure causes evictions and rate-limits silently reset, producing notification floods ('50 pushes in 10 min at the concert'). If using Cassandra: read latency on hot recipients (concerts, sports events) spikes to 50ms+, blocking the notifier and causing Kafka lag. User complaints about spam or about missing expected nearby alerts.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use Redis Cluster with `SET key val EX 21600 NX` for atomic check-and-set per (recipient, friend) pair, sharded by recipient_id; size to 200GB across 40 shards at 5GB each; aggregate sibling events in a 60s tumbling window per recipient so a user entering a dense friend cluster gets ONE 'N friends nearby' push instead of N pushes; fall back to per-recipient coarse bucket (1 push per recipient per hour regardless of friend) when token store is unavailable.
bottlenecks.detection: Metrics: rate_limit_store_memory_used_ratio (alert >75%), redis_evicted_keys_rate (alert >0 — evictions break correctness), pushes_per_recipient_per_hour p99 (alert >3 indicates aggregation failing), duplicate_push_complaint_rate from user feedback.

bottlenecks.title: Geofence check cost: GEODIST per candidate event amplifies Redis GEO load
bottlenecks.trigger: For every location event where a subscriber is offline, notifier calls `GEODIST` (or re-runs a 500m GEOSEARCH) to check proximity. At even 10% offline rate × 3.3M publishes/sec × 20 subscribers = ~6.6M extra Redis GEO ops/sec on top of the existing 3.3M GEOADD baseline — tripling load on the 20-shard Redis GEO cluster that's already at 165K ops/sec/shard.
bottlenecks.symptom: Redis GEO shards CPU saturates at >80%; GEOADD latency (hot path for publish!) degrades from <1ms to 10-50ms; publish pipeline backs up across the whole system, not just notifications. Notifier itself appears healthy but cripples an upstream dependency.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Skip the GEODIST entirely: the notifier already has the publisher's (lat, lng) in the Kafka record, and should maintain a cached last-known location per subscriber (from the same Kafka stream, LRU 10M entries) — compute haversine in-process, zero Redis calls; only consult Redis on cache miss. Alternatively, pre-filter in Subscription Manager: emit a lightweight `NEARBY_CANDIDATE` event to notifier only when fan-out already determined proximity.
bottlenecks.detection: Metrics: notifier_redis_geo_qps (alert >500K/sec aggregate — should be near zero with in-proc cache), geodist_cache_hit_ratio (alert <95%), correlation between notifier instance count and Redis GEO p99 latency (any positive correlation is a red flag).

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Notification Service is here For Nearby Friends, the WebSocket path only works when the app is *open*. But the most valuable moment in this product is exactly when it *isn't* — you're walking through a neighborhood and your phone is in your pocket when a friend happens to be two blocks away. Without something watching the location stream on behalf of offline users, that moment passes silently. The Notification Service is the piece that turns "Alice moved" into "Alice is now nearby" via APNs/FCM push, so users don't have to keep the app foregrounded to get value from it. ## What happens without it Strip this out and Nearby Friends becomes a map you have to be *already looking at* to learn anything new. Users open the app, see no one nearby, close it, and miss the friend who walked past 10 minutes later. Operators would see the WebSocket tier and fan-out humming along perfectly while engagement metrics crater — the system is technically working, it just has no way to reach a user whose app is backgrounded. ## The number The fan-out tier already processes **66M delivery events/sec** (3.3M publishes × 20 subscribers). The Notifier consumes the *same* Kafka stream but filters aggressively: roughly 10% of subscribers are offline, and of those only a small fraction have a friend inside the 500m geofence — maybe 1–5% of events survive filtering, so ~30–150K candidate pushes/sec. That's tractable for APNs/FCM if you pre-filter *before* calling the provider. ## The trade-off Dropped or delayed pushes are acceptable — notifications are best-effort, not the critical path.

operations.title: Publish my location (30s heartbeat)
operations.name: Publish my location (30s heartbeat)
operations.description: Client sends a LOC frame; server writes Redis GEO and emits to Kafka for fan-out. No response needed beyond an ACK.

steps.title: GPS fix triggers LOC frame
steps.action: Location provider fires after 30s or a 20m movement threshold, whichever comes first. Client encodes a protobuf LOC frame and writes it to the open WebSocket.
steps.note: Sent fire-and-forget — the client doesn't block waiting for an ACK; it just advances the seq counter.

steps.title: L4 LB relays the WS frame
steps.action: Connection is already established and consistent-hashed to a specific WS server. The LB is a passive pipe — no routing decision per frame.

steps.title: WS server decodes and validates
steps.action: Server decodes the protobuf, validates lat/lng bounds and ts skew, updates last_location in its in-process map, and hands off to the Location Publisher.
steps.codeOrCommand:
conn = connections[user_id] // in-process
assert -90 <= frame.lat <= 90
assert -180 <= frame.lng <= 180
assert abs(now - frame.ts) < 300 // ±5 min skew
conn.last_location = (frame.lat, frame.lng, frame.ts)
publisher.publish(user_id, frame.lat, frame.lng, frame.ts)

steps.title: Publisher writes Redis GEO and produces to Kafka
steps.action: Two parallel writes. Redis GEO is the authoritative current location for radius queries; Kafka drives the fan-out.

steps.title: Redis GEOADD
steps.action: Redis updates the sorted-set score (52-bit interleaved geohash) for member user_id=201. O(log N) — sub-millisecond in practice.
steps.codeOrCommand:
GEOADD locations:1 -122.4194 37.7749 201
# Internally: score = interleave52(geohash(lng,lat))
# ZADD locations:1 <score> 201
steps.note: Returns 0 because the member already existed (we only updated it). Returns 1 on first insert.

steps.title: Kafka append to partition
steps.action: Producer batches the record (linger.ms=10) with ~100 other location events, compresses, and sends to the partition leader. `acks=1` — leader ack suffices.

steps.title: Subscription Manager consumes the update
steps.action: One of the 200 consumer-group workers picks up the record and begins fan-out.
steps.codeOrCommand: for record in consumer.poll: publisher = record.value.user_id # 201 subs = friends_svc.subscribers_of(publisher) # cached for sub_id in subs: host = routing.lookup(sub_id) host.rpc_push(FRIEND_LOC, publisher, record.value)

steps.title: Subscriber list lookup (cache hit)
steps.action: Reverse index lookup: who has opted in to see user 201's location? Returns 20 user_ids. Hot-cached in-process; cache miss would hit Cassandra.
steps.codeOrCommand:
SELECT subscriber_id FROM subscribers_of WHERE friend_id = 201;
-- Result: [302, 415, 501, 777,...] (20 rows)
steps.decision: Cache hit — no Cassandra round trip

steps.title: Parallel push to 20 WS servers
steps.action: For each subscriber, look up which WS server hosts them (routing table) and fire a gRPC push. Fans out in parallel; individual failures NACKed and retried.
steps.codeOrCommand: with ThreadPool(20) as pool: pool.map(push_to_host, [ ("ws-17", 302), ("ws-42", 415), # same host as publisher — local call ("ws-88", 501),... ])

steps.title: WS servers deliver FRIEND_LOC to each subscriber
steps.action: Each receiving WS server finds the subscriber's open connection and writes the FRIEND_LOC frame. Subscribers that are offline are skipped (optional notification push handled separately).
steps.codeOrCommand:
conn = connections[sub_id]
if conn is None: return // offline — notifier will handle
conn.send(FrameFRIEND_LOC{ friend_id:201, lat:37.7749, lng:-122.4194, ts:1714000000 })
steps.decision: Subscriber online on this node — push direct; offline → notifier takes over

steps.title: Subscriber client moves the pin
steps.action: Receiving client decodes the frame and animates the friend's map pin to the new coordinates with a ~500ms tween.
steps.codeOrCommand: onFrame(frame): if frame.type == FRIEND_LOC: map.pins[frame.friend_id].animateTo(frame.lat, frame.lng, duration=500ms)

operations.title: Who of my friends is nearby right now? (radius query)
operations.name: Who of my friends is nearby right now? (radius query)
operations.description: User opens the Nearby Friends tab; client requests the current positions of friends within 5 miles.

steps.title: Open Nearby tab
steps.action: Client sends a NEARBY_QUERY frame with its own current position as the center.
steps.codeOrCommand: ws.send(NearbyQuery { lat: 37.7749, lng: -122.4194, radius_mi: 5 })

steps.title: LB relays to user's WS server
steps.action: Existing sticky connection.

steps.title: WS server fans out friend list + GEO query
steps.action: Server needs both the user's friend list AND the set of users within 5 miles, then intersects them.
steps.codeOrCommand:
friend_ids = friends_svc.friends_of(user_id) // parallel
nearby_ids = geo.geosearch(lat, lng, 5mi) // parallel
result = [f for f in friend_ids if f in nearby_ids]

steps.title: Friend list lookup
steps.action: Fetch all friends of the current user who have nearby_share=true.

steps.title: GEOSEARCH 5-mile radius
steps.action: Redis returns every user within 5 miles of (37.7749, -122.4194). Scans all 20 GEO shards in parallel.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# Query each shard
for shard in range(20): GEOSEARCH locations:{shard} FROMLONLAT -122.4194 37.7749 BYRADIUS 5 mi ASC COUNT 1000
# Aggregate results
steps.note: 40k people are within 5 miles in a dense city — that's why we intersect with the much smaller friend list next.

steps.title: WS server intersects and responds
steps.action: Set intersection: of 40k nearby users and 180 friends, maybe 4 are both. Server sends a NEARBY_RESULT frame.

steps.title: Render pins on map
steps.action: Client drops map pins for each returned friend and starts listening for live FRIEND_LOC updates.

operations.title: Friend comes online → fan-out PRESENCE
operations.name: Friend comes online → fan-out PRESENCE
operations.description: When a user opens the app, a PRESENCE frame fans out to subscribers so their UIs can un-grey the friend's pin.

steps.title: App foregrounded — open WebSocket
steps.action: Client sends HELLO with auth token.
steps.codeOrCommand:
ws = new WebSocket("wss://nearby.fb.com/")
ws.send(Hello { user_id:201, token:"..." })

steps.title: LB consistent-hashes to WS server
steps.action: user_id=201 hashes to ws-42. LB opens the upstream TCP.
steps.codeOrCommand: server = consistent_hash(user_id=201, ring=ws_pool) // ws-42

steps.title: WS server registers connection
steps.action: Server authenticates the token, writes user_id=201 → this_server_id into the shared etcd routing table, and emits a PRESENCE event to Kafka.
steps.codeOrCommand:
auth.verify(hello.token)
connections[201] = conn
etcd.put(f"/routes/{201}", f"ws-42", ttl=60s)
publisher.emit_presence(user_id=201, status=ONLINE)

steps.title: Presence event on Kafka
steps.action: A small PRESENCE record is written to the same `locations` stream (or a sibling `presence` topic, design choice).
steps.codeOrCommand: kafka.produce(topic="presence", key="201", value=PresenceEvent{user_id:201, status:ONLINE, ts:...})

steps.title: Subscription Manager fans out
steps.action: Same pattern as location fan-out: look up subscribers of 201, push PRESENCE to each.
steps.codeOrCommand:
subs = friends_svc.subscribers_of(201) // 20 users
for sub_id in subs: host = routing.lookup(sub_id) host.rpc_push(PRESENCE, friend_id=201, status=ONLINE)

steps.title: Subscriber WS servers forward PRESENCE frames
steps.action: Each receiving WS server pushes a PRESENCE frame to its locally-connected subscriber, if online.
steps.codeOrCommand: for sub_id in locally_connected(subscribers): conn.send(PresenceFrame{friend_id:201, status:ONLINE})
steps.decision: Subscriber online → deliver now; offline → skip (notifier may push ambient update)

steps.title: Optional push for offline subscribers
steps.action: Notifier checks for offline subscribers and decides whether a 'Alice is now nearby' alert is warranted (only if in 500m geofence and rate-limited).
steps.codeOrCommand: for sub_id in offline_subscribers: if rate_limit.ok(sub_id, 201, window=6h): dist = geo.geodist(locations, 201, sub_id, 'mi') if dist < 0.3: # 500m apns.send(sub_id, f"Alice is nearby ({dist:.1f} mi)")
steps.decision: Only push if close AND rate-limit allows — avoid notification fatigue

steps.title: Subscriber UI un-greys the pin
steps.action: Map pin for user 201 transitions from grey (offline) to color, optionally with a toast 'Alice is now nearby'.

tradeoffs.chosen: WebSocket over long-poll or gRPC streaming
tradeoffs.rationale: WebSocket is supported natively by every mobile OS and keeps a single connection per user so fanout is a map lookup. gRPC streaming works but adds a TLS plus HTTP2 dependency the mobile client would rather avoid.

tradeoffs.chosen: Redis Pub/Sub for hot path, Kafka for audit and replay
tradeoffs.rationale: Redis Pub/Sub is sub-millisecond but drops messages with no subscriber, which matches the 'zero retention' privacy requirement. Kafka behind it gives us a trail for abuse investigations without putting Kafka on the hot path.

tradeoffs.chosen: Check privacy at the router, not the ingestion server
tradeoffs.rationale: Ingestion has no friend graph context and checking there would force every WebSocket server to cache the entire social graph. The router already fetches the subscriber list, so adding the privacy mask is one extra boolean per delivery.

tradeoffs.chosen: Ephemeral in-memory quadtree plus Redis last-seen, no historical DB
tradeoffs.rationale: Storing every ping would create a surveillance dataset we do not want and explode storage cost. Latest-only in memory is cheaper and matches the product promise that 'we do not track your history'.

tradeoffs.chosen: Drop pings under load instead of queueing
tradeoffs.rationale: A queued ping that arrives 10 s late is misleading and worse than no ping. Dropping preserves the invariant that every delivered location is recent.
